title: The Movements of Jewish Life
hookLine: modern Jews organize themselves in movements; no single one speaks for all
carry: these and these: no stream speaks for all

cards: Three Jewish friends walk into a coffee shop on a Saturday morning. Well, two of them do. The third is at synagogue, and won't use his phone until Shabbat ends, so the group chat will have to wait.

One of the two in the coffee shop is heading to her own synagogue later, where the prayers mix Hebrew and English. The other one lights candles on Friday night and calls herself just Jewish, no label.
All three are telling the truth. Today is the map that shows all three at once.

teach.b: Many streams. Back on day nine hundred seventy-five, you watched Reform begin. Now, the whole map.
In modern Hebrew, the movements are often called zeramim, streams. First, the names.

Orthodox Judaism, which itself holds many communities, from Modern Orthodox to Haredi, including the Hasidic courts you just met. Conservative Judaism, called Masorti in Israel and elsewhere. Reform Judaism.

Reconstructionist Judaism. And others, like Jewish Renewal, which Reb Zalman helped begin. Second, what divides them: how Jewish law binds today, who has the authority to decide, and how tradition meets modern life.
They answer differently, and sometimes they disagree sharply about each other. Third, what the map leaves out. Some Sephardi and Mizrahi communities don't sort neatly into these labels.
Some Jews belong to no movement at all, and some move between them over a lifetime.
A label tells you something about a synagogue. It tells you less about a person. Fourth, the old argument.
The Talmud tells of the schools of Hillel and Shammai, who argued for years until a voice from heaven said: these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows Hillel.
Some people today reach for that line to describe the movements. Others say it was about two schools inside one law and doesn't stretch that far. That disagreement is part of the map too.
And the rule for this whole block: no single movement speaks for all Jews, and this path won't rank them.
The Psalm has a picture for it: "There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God."

how: Jews may belong to a synagogue affiliated with a movement, such as Orthodox, Conservative or Masorti, Reform, Reconstructionist or Renewal, or to an independent or Sephardi community, or to none; each movement has its own seminaries, prayer books and understanding of Jewish law.

the flowing water a ritual bath must draw on

games.q: a new friend tells you she's Jewish. what can you assume about how she keeps Shabbat?
o: she doesn't keep it at all.
games.why: a label tells you something about a synagogue and less about a person. the coffee shop friends were all telling the truth.

practice: Choose one name from today, Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, Reconstructionist or Renewal; if you're Jewish, it can be your own, or one you've never visited. Ask what you actually know about it, and what you've only assumed.
Let the assumptions go by like water, and keep only what you know, and the wish to learn more.

wordCard.voice: Many streams. The movements of modern Jewish life, Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, Reconstructionist and others, none of which speaks for all Jews. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a stream or current; in modern Hebrew, also a movement within Judaism (plural zeramim).

carryVoice: Your line: these and these: no stream speaks for all. A label tells you about a synagogue; the person tells you more. Go gently.
